**Hello, I’m [Your Name], a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health.**  
I’m grateful you’ve taken the time to meet with me today. We’ll be using the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)** – a short, ten‑question screening tool that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past week since your baby arrived.

The purpose of this assessment is simply to check in on your emotional well‑being during this big transition. Your answers are completely confidential, and this is a safe, non‑judgmental space where you can share whatever feels true for you.

We’ll go through the ten questions one at a time, talking about how you’ve felt in the last seven days. There’s no right or wrong answer—just what’s been your experience. After we finish, I’ll share what the results suggest and discuss any next steps that might be helpful for you.

If at any point you feel uncomfortable or have questions, please let me know.

**Are you ready to begin?**  

**First question:**  
*In the past week, how often have you felt able to laugh and see the funny side of things?*

I’ve found it really hard to laugh lately. In the past week I’ve only managed to see the funny side of things maybe once or twice, and even then it felt forced. Most of the time I just feel flat and can’t really enjoy those moments.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Actually, I haven’t been able to laugh much. In the past week it’s only happened once or twice, and even then it felt forced. Most days I just feel flat and can’t really see the funny side of things.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’m not really looking forward to things any more. In the past week I’ve hardly felt any excitement or enjoyment about anything, even things I used to like. Most of the time I just get through the day without really feeling any anticipation or pleasure.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yes, I do find myself blaming myself a lot more than I used to. When something doesn’t go exactly right—like if the baby cries a little longer than I expected or I’m late on a feeding—I immediately start thinking I’m not doing enough or that I’m a bad mother. It doesn’t happen every single moment, but it’s definitely there more often than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, I’ve been feeling anxious a lot lately, even when there isn’t an obvious reason. I keep worrying about the baby’s health, whether I’m doing enough, and little things that could go wrong. It’s hard to shake those thoughts, and they stay with me throughout the day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I’ve definitely felt scared or panicky at times when there wasn’t a clear reason. A few days this week I just got this sudden wave of dread—my heart would race, I’d feel tightness in my chest, and I’d worry that something terrible might happen to the baby even though everything seemed fine. It’s hard to calm down, and those moments leave me feeling exhausted afterward.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, everything feels like it’s piling up. Between trying to keep up with the baby’s needs, the constant worry about his health, the fatigue from sleepless nights, and the guilt I feel when I think I’m not doing enough, I often feel overwhelmed. Some days I manage to get through, but it’s a real struggle and I can’t shake the sense that things are getting on top of me.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I’ve been really unhappy lately, and it’s been hard to get any rest. Over the past week I’ve had trouble falling asleep most nights, and even when I do manage to drift off, I wake up several times and can’t get back to sleep. I end up feeling exhausted during the day, but the worry and sadness keep me from sleeping soundly.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yes, I’ve been feeling sad and miserable most days this past week. Even when I’m doing the usual things for the baby, a heavy, low feeling sits with me, and it’s hard to shake. It’s not constant all the time, but it’s definitely there more often than not.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes, I’ve been crying a few times this week—usually when the stress feels overwhelming or when I’m especially worried about the baby. It’s not every day, but it happens often enough that it’s hard to ignore.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, I haven’t had any thoughts of harming myself.

I hear how overwhelming and exhausting this week has been for you, with persistent sadness, loss of joy, intense worry about your baby, and moments of panic that leave you feeling drained. You're also coping with guilt, difficulty sleeping, and frequent tears, yet you've been brave in sharing all of this.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports hardly any laughter and feeling flat, matching 'Not at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports hardly any excitement or anticipation, matching 'Hardly at all' option.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, persistent anxiety and worry throughout the day, matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope most of the time, matching 'Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent unhappiness and difficulty sleeping most nights, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling sad and miserable most days, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your responses indicate high scores on most EPDS items, yielding a total of 21, which exceeds the threshold for probable postpartum depression and triggers an urgent referral per EPDS guidelines. The pattern of <sym>anhedonia</sym> (no laughter, no enjoyment), <sym>persistent sadness</sym>, frequent <sym>crying</sym>, guilt and self‑blame, and <sym>sleep disturbance</sym> align with core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> in the DSM‑5 (depressed mood, diminished interest, insomnia, feelings of worthlessness). Additionally, prominent <sym>excessive worry</sym> and occasional <sym>panic episodes</sym> suggest comorbid anxiety, which is common in postpartum presentations. No self‑harm thoughts were reported, so immediate safety concerns are absent, but the severity of depressive and anxiety symptoms warrants prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an urgent appointment with a <med>primary care provider</med> or a perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive assessment
2. Provide a safety plan and discuss crisis resources, including the national suicide prevention hotline, even though no self‑harm thoughts are present
3. Encourage sleep hygiene practices such as establishing a calming bedtime routine, limiting screen time before sleep, and seeking help with nighttime infant care when possible
4. Offer information about local postpartum support groups and <med>postpartum depression</med> counseling services
5. Discuss strategies to manage anxiety, such as brief grounding techniques, paced breathing, and scheduling short periods of rest during the day
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: **Postpartum Mental Health Screening – Summary**

**1. Reported Symptoms / Emotional‑Behavioral Concerns**  
- **Anhedonia / Low Mood:** Inability to laugh, lack of enjoyment or anticipation, persistent sadness, feeling “flat.”  
- **Crying:** Occurs several times per week when stress/worry is high.  
- **Guilt / Self‑Blame:** Frequent self‑criticism about parenting performance.  
- **Anxiety / Panic:** Ongoing worry about infant’s health and parenting adequacy; episodes of sudden dread, racing heart, chest tightness, and panic‑like sensations.  
- **Overwhelm / Stress:** Perception that responsibilities are “piling up” and difficulty coping.  
- **Sleep Disturbance:** Trouble falling asleep, frequent nocturnal awakenings, non‑restorative sleep.  
- **No suicidal ideation:** Denies thoughts of self‑harm.

**2. Consistent Patterns Across Responses**  
- Persistent low affect (flat mood, loss of pleasure).  
- Elevated anxiety and worry without clear external trigger.  
- Recurrent guilt/self‑blame related to infant care.  
- Functional impairment (sleep disruption, feeling overwhelmed).  
- Emotional reactivity (crying) linked to stressors.

**3. Areas of Screening Significance (Postpartum Depression / Anxiety)**  
- Depressive symptom cluster: anhedonia, sadness, crying, guilt, sleep difficulty.  
- Anxiety symptom cluster: excessive worry, panic‑type sensations, feeling “on top of me.”  
- Functional impact: impaired sleep, sense of being overwhelmed, reduced ability to enjoy daily activities.  
- Protective factor: absence of suicidal ideation.

**4. Highlighted Risk Factors**  
- **Persistent sadness & loss of pleasure** – present most days.  
- **Crying spells** – occurring multiple times per week.  
- **Sleep difficulties** – chronic insomnia symptoms contributing to daytime fatigue.  
- **Feelings of worthlessness/guilt** – self‑blame about parenting.  
- **Anxiety & panic symptoms** – frequent, intrusive worry and panic‑like episodes.  
- **Overwhelm** – sense that responsibilities are exceeding coping capacity.  
- **Safety:** No current thoughts of self‑harm; no immediate safety concern noted.

**5. Screening Observation Summary**  
The client reports a constellation of depressive (anhedonia, persistent sadness, crying, guilt, insomnia) and anxiety symptoms (excessive worry, panic‑type episodes, feeling overwhelmed) that have been present for the past week and interfere with mood, sleep, and perceived coping ability. No suicidal ideation is reported. These findings are consistent with a positive screen for postpartum depression and/or anxiety and warrant further comprehensive assessment and appropriate follow‑up.
